title: What if the network was the sandbox? — Remy Guercio, Tailscale

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's central thesis is moving authN and authZ to the network layer to eliminate credential exfiltration risk for AI agents, with guardrails, identity, and access control as the driving concerns. Aperture is a developer-facing LLM gateway platform for securing agent access across multiple providers, applicable to any application vertical. The talk demonstrates a deployed gateway in active production use with operational visibility, while some guardrails remain planned for future implementation. Requires familiarity with WireGuard, Tailscale, OIDC, and LLM gateway concepts but remains accessible to AI engineering practitioners. A conference presentation featuring live product demonstrations and audience Q&A. All classification claims are directly supported by statements in the transcript with grade said_in_transcript.

summary: Remy Guercio begins by deconstructing a sandbox into two components: a boundary (inside vs. outside) and a set of permissions (what the sandbox can access). He argues that current permission handling for agents falls into two camps—API keys (favored by model labs, full price, no real authN/authZ distinction) and OAuth/OIDC (more cost-effective but still places credentials inside the sandbox). In both cases the agent holds its own permissions, creating exfiltration and misuse risk, especially for long-running loops. He introduces Tailscale, built on WireGuard, which attaches identity—user, groups, or tags—to every network connection, enabling network-level authN and authZ. He presents Aperture, Tailscale's AI gateway: a single provider key (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, etc.) is placed on Aperture, and agents connect through it with no real key in their sandbox—only a dummy dash placeholder. Agent setup is minimal: a dummy API key and a base URL pointing to Aperture, working across Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI. In a live demo, Guercio shows Aperture's dashboard with per-identity usage metrics, token counts, cost per model, and full request/response inspection including headers and bodies. Because every LLM call passes through the network gateway, Aperture sees every tool call, bash command, grep, and MCP request without in-container instrumentation. He demonstrates this on a dogfood PR review bot, showing MCP tool calls, bash commands, and grep operations. He shows a 10-word story demo that drifts from robots to dogs to cats over weeks and notes the model cannot count to ten. Aperture supports cross-provider cost controls, per-identity quotas (e.g., $5/day), and webhooks that fire on every tool call—guaranteed because traffic must pass through the gateway. Aperture is built on identity primitives available via tsnet, an open source Go library for custom identity-aware services on the tailnet. In Q&A, Guercio explains permission configuration via both a visual grants editor and Tailscale's ACL policy file. He explains base URLs are explicitly configured rather than transparently intercepted. He notes permissions are currently model/provider-based with user-based permissioning in progress, and budgets can be unioned or differentiated by provider (e.g., unlimited internal GPU but limited Opus 4.6). When asked about agents moving away from structured tool calls toward direct code execution, he explains they chose the LLM layer over the MCP layer because code still gets run and LLM-layer visibility captures it; internally at Tailscale, bash dominates over everything else. Future guardrails for bash commands (e.g., blocking rm -rf /) are planned. The core rationale: if you can't see everything, how valuable is the gateway?
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: Sandboxing conflates two distinct problems: execution isolation and access control; you can isolate a runtime yet still leave credentials vulnerable inside it.
Both API keys and OIDC place credentials inside the sandbox, giving agents something to exfiltrate or misuse, especially in long-running loops.
Tailscale's WireGuard-based network attaches verified identity (user, group, or tag) to every connection, enabling network-level authN and authZ.
Aperture is an LLM gateway that holds the single provider key; agents in sandboxes connect with a dummy key and a base URL, eliminating exfiltration risk.
Because all LLM traffic flows through Aperture, it sees every tool call, bash command, grep, and MCP request without instrumenting the container.
Aperture chose the LLM layer over the MCP layer because even when agents write and execute code directly, the LLM call still passes through the gateway.
Internally at Tailscale, bash commands dominate over structured tool calls and MCP—Aperture makes this visible for the first time.
Aperture provides cross-provider cost controls, per-identity quotas, webhooks on every tool call, and future bash guardrails (e.g., blocking rm -rf /).
tsnet, Tailscale's open source Go library, lets anyone build identity-aware internal services including MCP servers on the tailnet without OAuth.
Permissions are currently model/provider-based with user and group-based permissioning in progress; budgets can be unioned or differentiated by provider.

sections.title: Introduction and the concept of a sandbox
sections.summary: Guercio introduces the talk's central question: what if the network served as the sandbox? He frames the discussion around rethinking sandboxing at the network layer and previews a demo of a project Tailscale is building.

sections.title: Components of a sandbox: boundary and permissions
sections.summary: He breaks a sandbox into two components: a boundary (thing in vs. thing out) and a set of permissions. Without permissions or identity, a sandbox is empty—'a sandbox without any toys.'

sections.title: How permissions are typically handled: API keys vs. OIDC
sections.summary: He describes two current approaches: API keys (preferred by model labs, full price, conflates authN and authZ, exfiltration risk especially in long-running loops) and OAuth/OIDC (more cost-effective but still places credentials inside the sandbox). In both cases the agent has access to its own permissions.

sections.title: Tailscale and WireGuard for network-level identity
sections.summary: He introduces Tailscale, built on WireGuard, which gives every node on a network a set of keys and layers identity on top. Each connection carries the user, groups, or tags, enabling network-level authN and authZ for containers, GPU servers, laptops, and more.

sections.title: Introduction to Aperture (AI Gateway)
sections.summary: He introduces Aperture as an LLM gateway on the tailnet. A single provider key (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, Vertex, Bedrock) is placed on Aperture. Agents in sandboxes connect through it with no key of their own. GitHub Actions runners use federated OIDC to join the tailnet with a tag that determines their Aperture permissions.

sections.title: Live demo: Usage metrics and logs in Aperture
sections.summary: He demonstrates Aperture in light mode, showing per-identity usage metrics: tokens used, models used, money spent, and individual requests. He drills into a Claude Code session, showing full request headers and response bodies, noting that even 'say hello' costs ~20 cents due to large system context.

sections.title: Live demo: Inspecting GitHub Actions PR review bot logs
sections.summary: He shows a dogfood PR review bot with a tag, displaying 30 days of history. He inspects individual requests showing cost (e.g., 4 cents), bash commands executed, and multiple simultaneous commands.

sections.title: Tool call visibility at the network layer
sections.summary: He emphasizes that all tool calls—MCP requests, bash commands, grep—must pass through Aperture, giving a guarantee of full visibility without in-container instrumentation. If access is cut off, the agent sees only a dead key, not an error it can route around.

sections.title: Agent setup and configuration in Aperture
sections.summary: He shows the minimal agent setup: in Claude Code, a dummy API key (a dash) and a base URL pointing to Aperture. This works across Codex, Claude Code, and Gemini CLI. He demonstrates his own settings.json and runs a 10-word story prompt, noting model behavior drift over weeks (robots to dogs to cats) and the model's inability to count to 10.

sections.title: Request inspection and pipeline debugging
sections.summary: He returns to the logs to show a three-request session for the 10-word story, including the initial 20-cent request, a follow-up 'are you sure' request, and a correction. He emphasizes that when things break in PR review bots, Aperture logs let you trace what happened.

sections.title: Advanced features: Cost controls, quotas, and webhooks
sections.summary: He describes cross-provider cost controls where a single budget works across all providers rather than per-provider allocation. Per-identity quotas (e.g., $5/day) are available. Webhooks fire on every tool call with full information to third-party services—guaranteed because traffic must pass through the gateway.

sections.title: Using tsnet to build custom internal identity-aware services
sections.summary: He explains that Aperture is built on Tailscale identity primitives available via tsnet, an open source Go library. Anyone can write a Go program that joins the tailnet, reads identity information, and builds custom internal MCP servers or API endpoints without OAuth. Aperture itself could theoretically be rebuilt using these same primitives. It is available on Tailscale's free plan.

sections.title: Q&A: How to configure permissions (Grants vs. ACLs)
sections.summary: He explains permissions can be configured in two places: a visual grants editor (with groups coming soon) for model access, quotas, MCP access, hooks, and roles; and Tailscale's ACL policy file, which supports application capabilities—arbitrary metadata sent with identity. Both visual and JSON/GitOps workflows are supported via the API.

sections.title: Q&A: Network-layer transparency for base URLs
sections.summary: Asked whether base URLs could be transparently intercepted at the network layer, he explains this was discussed but they chose explicit configuration for simplicity. Transparent interception can break and confuse things. The goal is to make LLM access easy for developers while giving security teams visibility and controls.

sections.title: Q&A: Permissioning based on users vs. model/provider
sections.summary: He notes that currently permissioning is model/provider-based. User and group-based permissioning (e.g., 'this team gets this budget') is in progress, with the same system applying to quotas and budgets, not just model access.

sections.title: Q&A: Budget unions and provider-specific limits
sections.summary: He elaborates that budgets can be unioned across dimensions—for example, an individual gets a smaller budget, or unlimited access to internal GPU endpoints but a limited amount for Opus 4.6. This flexibility in combining per-user and per-model limits is part of the planned user-based permissioning.

sections.title: Q&A: Permissioning when agents execute code directly
sections.summary: Asked how permissioning works when agents move away from structured tool calls toward writing and executing code directly, he acknowledges this is more complicated but explains it is the whole reason they chose the LLM layer over the MCP layer: even with code execution, agents are still typically running something, and the LLM call still passes through Aperture. He reveals that internally at Tailscale, bash dominates over everything else in tool usage. Many customers just want visibility into what tools are being used before worrying about blocking. Future guardrails for bash commands (e.g., blocking rm -rf /) are planned. The core rationale is that if you can't see everything, the gateway's value is limited, so they chose the layer that captures the most.
